title: The Economics of Your Life
objective: After this level you can apply the tree's big ideas to everyday choices about work, saving and spending.
summary: Keynes's 15-hour week never came, but longer retirements added leisure. Defaults shape how people save, and the sunk cost effect shows spent money steering choices.

cards.headline: Big ideas, small choices: your job, your savings, tonight's ticket.
cards.body: Economics isn't only about nations and markets. Its ideas show up in how much you work, whether you save, and whether you sit through a play you're not enjoying.

cards.headline: Work: Keynes's 15-hour week
cards.body: In 1930, Keynes predicted that a century later, living standards would be four to eight times higher and people might work just 15 hours a week. Economist Nicholas Crafts concluded the short week won't arrive by 2030. But the free time turned up somewhere else: in the UK, expected lifetime hours of leisure and home production rose 58% between 1931 and 2011, reflecting longer lives and longer retirements.

cards.headline: Saving: the power of the default
cards.body: Behavioral economists find that small details shape big decisions. One is the default: what happens unless you actively choose something else. Another is timing. Promising to save more in the future, especially after a raise, feels easier than saving more today, and Thaler and Shlomo Benartzi built their Save More Tomorrow plan on that. Critics call such nudges paternalistic; supporters stress that joining is voluntary and you can opt out any time.

cards.fact: Paying full price made people go to more plays.
cards.context: In a 1985 study, Hal Arkes and Catherine Blumer sold theater season tickets at full price or at random discounts. Over the next six months, the full-price buyers went to more plays, though the money was spent either way. That's the sunk cost effect: a greater tendency to keep going with something once money, effort or time has gone into it.

mascot.line: Paid full price, so you'd better go? The study suggests that's exactly how our heads work.

cards.headline: Economics, up close
learned: Keynes's 15-hour week never came, but retirement did
Defaults and timing shape how much people save
Sunk costs can steer choices they shouldn't
Big ideas show up in small decisions

questions.prompt: What did Keynes predict in 1930 for a century later?

options.label: Falling living standards and longer hours
options.rationale: He predicted the opposite on both counts.

options.label: Much higher living standards and a 15-hour work week
The end of money
options.rationale: His essay was about wealth and work, not abolishing money.

options.label: A return to the gold standard
options.rationale: The essay was about living standards and leisure.

questions.explanation: Keynes predicted living standards four to eight times higher and a 15-hour week; the short week hasn't arrived.

questions.prompt: In Arkes and Blumer's study, why did full-price ticket holders go to more plays?

options.label: Their seats were better
options.rationale: The only difference was the price, set at random.

options.label: The plays they chose were better
options.rationale: Everyone had the same season of plays.

options.label: Money already spent pushed them to keep going
They got refunds for missed plays
options.rationale: No refunds: the money was spent either way.

questions.explanation: That is the sunk cost effect: past spending that can't be recovered still steers what people do next.

questions.prompt: From Level 1: Save More Tomorrow helps people use money for which of its three jobs?

options.label: Medium of exchange
options.rationale: That's the job money does when you spend it.

options.label: Unit of account
options.rationale: That's the job of pricing things.

options.label: Double coincidence of wants
options.rationale: That's barter's matching problem from Level 2.

questions.explanation: Saving money to use later is its job as a store of value, which Save More Tomorrow encourages.
